lines.text: What if you could open a folder on your laptop, type one message, and a whole software team gets to work?
Not one chatbot. A team.
A developer, a designer, a reviewer and a tester, all working on your project.
That is Octopus.
And today I'll show you a real run, start to finish. Nothing staged.
Most AI coding tools work like one very fast intern.
You ask, it writes, and then you check everything yourself.
But real software is not built like that.
Real teams split the work. Someone builds. Someone reviews the code. Someone checks the design.
And someone actually clicks through the product before it ships.
Octopus copies that structure.
You talk to one team lead, called Octopus.
It reads your request, writes it down as numbered requirements, and hires the specialists the job needs.
Then the cycle runs. Plan, build, review, verify, and report.
Every part has one owner, and nothing is called done until someone has checked it.
Let's see it working. This is the actual Octopus app, running locally on this machine.
First, the model. I paste my Azure OpenAI endpoint, add the key, and save.
Then, test connection.
Connected to GPT 6 Luna, in under two seconds.
And the key stays encrypted on this computer. It is never sent back to the browser.
Now, the request.
I'm asking for a landing page for Chai Tapri, a small chai cafe in Bengaluru.
A warm hero section, a menu with prices in rupees, an order counter where I can add and remove cups, and a contact section with opening hours.
Responsive, and plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
I give it an empty folder, create the project, and send.
Within fifteen seconds, Octopus has turned my message into seven requirements, in my own words.
Then it hires.
Maya, a frontend developer. Ira, a UI and UX designer. And Dev, a QA engineer.
Look at the canvas. The org chart builds itself as each person joins, grouped into engineering, design, and quality.
Maya owns the whole page, so she builds it end to end.
She writes the HTML, then the styles, then the script.
She checks the JavaScript, starts a small local server, and opens the page in a real browser.
She clicks plus and minus on the menu, reads the totals back, and resizes the window to test mobile.
All of this, before she even says she is done.
When Maya finishes, the reviewers step in, in parallel.
Kai, the tech lead, reviews the code.
Ira opens the page at desktop and phone widths, and judges the design.
And Dev, the QA engineer, play-tests the edge cases, at six screen widths, and with the keyboard alone.
All three of them sign off. If anyone had asked for changes, the notes would go back to Maya together, in one revision.
Then comes the part I like the most.
A verifier runs the actual product, and judges every requirement with evidence.
On the first try, Dev could not open the running page. So he did not tick the boxes.
He marked them as not met, and the work went back to Maya.
She added a proper start command, and Dev checked again.
This time, seven out of seven requirements met, each one with a note on how it was tested.
The whole run took about fifteen minutes.
Five agents. One hundred and thirteen model calls. Two point four million tokens.
And the cost, shown live in the header, five rupees and forty nine paise.
That is cheaper than one cutting chai.
So, what came out?
Here is the page, exactly as the team left it.
A deep green hero, with a little chai glass drawn entirely in CSS.
The menu, with cutting chai at fifteen rupees, and filter coffee at twenty five.
Let me add three cutting chai, and two ginger chai.
The order card updates right away. Eighty five rupees, total.
Scroll down, and there's the contact section, with the opening hours.
And on a phone, everything stacks neatly into one column.
Now, these agents work in your real folder. So the server enforces the limits, not the model.
Every file is versioned, and the Changes view lets you revert any of them in one click.
Agent commands are checked before they run, and they never see your keys. Dangerous ones, like R M, or git reset hard, are simply refused.
And the app only listens on your own machine.
One more thing. Octopus does not pretend.
Two follow-up tasks stayed open in this run, and the report says so, right below the requirements table.
You always see what actually happened.
You ask. The team plans, builds, reviews and verifies.
You get an honest report, and the same team is ready for your next message.
That's Octopus. Your AI company, in one folder.
